explanations.explanation: Shechem, baker. Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel there (Joshua 24:1). Every tribe, plus the elders, leaders, judges and officers, all in one place. That's a lot of sandals to line up at the door.

Gilgal's a good name to have in your pocket, but this gathering isn't there. The text says Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel at Shechem (Joshua 24:1). Hold onto Shechem, because it comes back later in this chapter.

Bethel is a name a lot of people know, but the text puts this gathering somewhere else. Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel at Shechem (Joshua 24:1). Shechem comes back later, when Joshua makes a covenant for the people there (Joshua 24:25). So Shechem is the name to keep.

True. Joshua summoned the elders, leaders, judges and officers of Israel, and they presented themselves before God (Joshua 24:1). That's more than a crowd showing up for a meeting, friend. I think the room went a little quiet when they stood there.

Here's what the text says: Joshua summoned the elders, leaders, judges and officers of Israel, and they presented themselves before God (Joshua 24:1). So the statement holds up. Joshua gathers everyone, and they come before God, not just before him. This one had no trick in it, baker.

The text says the opposite, friend. Terah and Nahor lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods (Joshua 24:2). So the LORD opens with where the family came from, and it wasn't a spotless start. The good news is that the story doesn't stay there.

You got it, baker. The LORD says Israel's fathers, including Terah the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods (Joshua 24:2). That's the family's starting line. I think it matters, because Joshua later tells the people to cast aside the gods their fathers served (Joshua 24:14).

Isaac, baker. The LORD says, "I gave him Isaac…" (Joshua 24:3). Abraham is led through all the land of Canaan and his descendants are multiplied, and Isaac is the next name on the family tree. If you can hold onto that name, you're doing better than I do finding my hat, and it's sitting right on my head.
Laban doesn't show up in this verse. The LORD says, "I gave him Isaac…" (Joshua 24:3). That's the son given to Abraham here. Laban is a name for another day, friend.

Jethro isn't named anywhere in this chapter. The LORD says, "I gave him Isaac…" (Joshua 24:3), and that's the gift to Abraham in this verse. There are a lot of names floating around the Bible, so it's easy to grab a different one off the shelf. The verse will point you to the right one every time.

Jacob goes in the first blank. The LORD says, "to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau" (Joshua 24:4). Esau got Mount Seir to possess, while Jacob and his sons took a different road, down to Egypt. Two brothers, two directions.

Egypt belongs in the second blank. Esau got Mount Seir to possess, but Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt (Joshua 24:4). Down is the word the text uses. And Egypt is where this family's story is headed next, because the LORD goes on to bring Israel out of there (Joshua 24:5).

Joseph is a name that belongs to this family, but verse 4 doesn't use it. The LORD says He gave Isaac Jacob and Esau (Joshua 24:4). Joseph does show up later in this chapter, when his bones are buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). Good name, different spot.

Moab turns up in this chapter as the kingdom of Balak (Joshua 24:9). It isn't where Jacob's family went. Verse 4 says Esau got Mount Seir, and Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt. Let's save Moab for Balak's turn.

Babylon never appears in this chapter. The text says Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt, while Esau got Mount Seir to possess (Joshua 24:4). Sorry, Babylon, no ticket today. Egypt is the one this verse names.

The text doesn't say that, friend. Israel's fathers cried out to the LORD, and He put darkness between them and the Egyptians (Joshua 24:7). Nobody swings a sword in that verse. They cry out, and He steps in.

You got it, baker. Israel's fathers didn't turn and fight. They cried out to the LORD, and He put darkness between them and the Egyptians, then brought the sea over the Egyptians (Joshua 24:7). I'd have panicked, honestly, and my mustache would have tied itself in a knot.

Darkness. The LORD says, "He put darkness between you and the Egyptians…" (Joshua 24:7). After that, He brought the sea over the Egyptians and engulfed them. The fathers cried out, and the LORD answered. That's the order the verse gives.

Hail makes for a dramatic guess, but verse 7 doesn't use it. The text says He put darkness between Israel and the Egyptians (Joshua 24:7). Then He brought the sea over the Egyptians. Stick with the word the verse gives you, friend.

Thunder is a loud pick, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says He put darkness between Israel and the Egyptians (Joshua 24:7). Then the sea came over the Egyptians. Quiet darkness, baker, and no thunder.
Curse. Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent for Balaam son of Beor "to curse you" (Joshua 24:9). That's the plan on paper. We'll see how that plan holds up in the very next verse.
Count is a quiet word, but the text says Balak sent for Balaam to curse Israel (Joshua 24:9). A king doesn't usually send for someone just to do his paperwork. His goal was a curse, friend.
Warn doesn't fit what the verse says. Balak, king of Moab, sent for Balaam "to curse you" (Joshua 24:9). He wanted a curse, plain and simple. Warning Israel isn't in the text.

The text says the opposite. The LORD says, "I would not listen to Balaam" (Joshua 24:10). So Balaam blessed Israel again and again, and the LORD delivered Israel from his hand. Balak sent for a curse and got blessings, which is a rough delivery day for a king.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "I would not listen to Balaam," and Balaam blessed Israel again and again (Joshua 24:10). Balak wanted one thing and got the reverse, over and over. That plan had one job, and it did the opposite.

explanations.answer: The LORD delivers them into Israel's hand
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The people of Jericho fought against Israel, and so did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites and Jebusites (Joshua 24:11). Then the LORD says, "I delivered them into your hand." That's Jericho's people plus seven more names on the opposing side, and the verse still ends the same way.

explanations.answer: Israel makes a peace treaty with them
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a treaty. It says Jericho and those nations fought against Israel, and the LORD says, "I delivered them into your hand" (Joshua 24:11). No paperwork to sign in this verse. It ends with the LORD delivering them.

explanations.answer: Israel retreats back across the Jordan
explanations.explanation: No retreat in this verse. Israel crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho, and when the people of Jericho and the other nations fought, the LORD says, "I delivered them into your hand" (Joshua 24:11). Israel doesn't head back across anything. They're already in the land.

The LORD says the opposite, friend. He says, "I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your own sword or bow" (Joshua 24:12). Sword and bow get no credit here. I think they'd file a complaint.

You got it, baker. The LORD says the hornet drove out the two Amorite kings, "but not by your own sword or bow" (Joshua 24:12). So the credit doesn't go to Israel's aim. It goes to the One who sent the hornet.

Yes, friend. Joshua says, "cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:14). That connects back to the start of the LORD's words, where Terah and Nahor worshiped other gods beyond the Euphrates (Joshua 24:2). It's not a shelf-tidying job. It's a choice about who they serve.

Riches aren't on Joshua's list. He tells them to fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth, and to "cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt" (Joshua 24:14). The things on the chopping block are gods, baker. Not treasure.

Weapons don't come up here. Joshua says, "cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:14). The LORD had just said the land wasn't won by their own sword or bow anyway (Joshua 24:12). The thing to put down is the gods.

Yes, baker. Joshua says, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" (Joshua 24:15). No hedging and no "let me check my calendar." He lays out the choice and then tells them exactly where he stands.
Joshua doesn't hedge like that. He says, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" (Joshua 24:15). Wait and see is how I treat a batch in the oven, and even then I peek every two minutes.

The elders are in the room (Joshua 24:1), but Joshua's answer isn't about them. He says, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" (Joshua 24:15). His house is serving the LORD. That's the answer.

explanations.answer: He protected them throughout their journey
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The people say, "He also protected us throughout our journey and among all the nations through which we traveled" (Joshua 24:17). They bring receipts. Egypt, the great signs, and the protection all go in their list.

explanations.answer: He left them on their own after that
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what they say, friend. They say, "He also protected us throughout our journey and among all the nations through which we traveled" (Joshua 24:17). They don't describe being on their own. They describe being protected.

explanations.answer: He gave them a king to lead them
explanations.explanation: A king isn't on their list. They say He brought them out of Egypt, performed great signs before their eyes, and "protected us throughout our journey" (Joshua 24:17). Those are the reasons they give. Leave the king out of this one, baker.

explanations.answer: You are not able to serve the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what Joshua says, baker. "You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God…" (Joshua 24:19). Talk about a record scratch. They just promised, and Joshua doesn't clap. I think he wants them to feel how big that promise is.

explanations.answer: The LORD is pleased with you today
explanations.explanation: That's not what Joshua says. He tells them, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God…" (Joshua 24:19). It's a surprise after such a big promise, friend. Nothing in the verse says the LORD is pleased.

explanations.answer: You must first build Him an altar
explanations.explanation: Joshua doesn't mention an altar here. His words are, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God…" (Joshua 24:19). He goes straight to what kind of God the LORD is. No building project, baker.
The people don't back down, friend. They answer, "No! We will serve the LORD!" (Joshua 24:21). Joshua said they couldn't, and they said no right back. They hold their ground.
You got it, baker. After Joshua says they can't, the people reply, "No! We will serve the LORD!" (Joshua 24:21). They hold their promise, and they say it louder. No backing up in this verse.

Witnesses. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:22). And the people answer, "We are witnesses!" They basically signed their own statement, baker.

Judges are in this chapter, because Joshua summoned them with the elders, leaders and officers (Joshua 24:1). But here the word is witnesses. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:22). Judges are a different job, friend.

Strangers doesn't fit, because these people aren't outsiders to the choice. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:22). They're the ones who chose. So they're witnesses to their own words.

They don't refuse, friend. When Joshua says they are witnesses against themselves, they answer, "We are witnesses!" (Joshua 22:22 is not it, it's Joshua 24:22). They say it quick and loud. No fine print.

You got it, baker. Joshua tells them, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD," and they say, "We are witnesses!" (Joshua 24:22). They agree on the spot. Nobody takes a step back.

explanations.answer: They will serve the LORD and obey His voice
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The people say, "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice" (Joshua 24:24). They keep saying they'll serve Him, but this time they add something: obey His voice. It's a promise with a bit more to it.

explanations.answer: They will think it over until morning
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show them stalling. They say to Joshua, "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice" (Joshua 24:24). No asking for time in this verse. They answer him.

explanations.answer: They will decide once each tribe meets
explanations.explanation: No tribal meetings are mentioned. The people say to Joshua, "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice" (Joshua 24:24). They answer him directly, friend. No committee needed.

A stone, baker. Joshua took a large stone and set it up under the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD (Joshua 24:26). He recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God and then set up the stone. Paper and stone, that's a double filing system.
No altar in this verse, friend. Joshua took a large stone and set it up under the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD (Joshua 24:26). That's the thing he sets up. Stone is the word to fill the blank.

A lampstand doesn't appear in these verses. The text says Joshua took a large stone and set it up under the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD (Joshua 24:26). A big stone is what stands there. The blank wants stone, baker.

explanations.answer: It has heard all the LORD's words to them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Joshua gives, baker. He says, "for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us" (Joshua 24:27). He adds that it will be a witness against them if they ever deny their God. A stone sits there and remembers, and that's its whole job.

explanations.answer: It was carried up from the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Joshua never says where the stone came from. His reason is, "for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us" (Joshua 24:27). It's a witness because of what it heard. Not because of where it's been.

explanations.answer: Moses carved the Law into it
explanations.explanation: Moses and carving don't come up here. Joshua says the stone will be a witness "for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us" (Joshua 24:27). Joshua is the one who recorded things in the Book of the Law of God (Joshua 24:26). The stone's reason is what it heard, friend.
110. Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110 (Joshua 24:29). I think this one hurts a little, and that's okay. It's a quiet moment, and it's good to let it be one, baker.

The text says Joshua died at 110 (Joshua 24:29). You may be thinking of Moses, who was 120 when he died (Deuteronomy 34:7). I think this is a tender verse, friend. Joshua is called the servant of the LORD.
Joshua died at the age of 110 (Joshua 24:29). The number 175 belongs to Abraham, who died at that age (Genesis 25:7). This is a heavy verse, baker. Joshua is called the servant of the LORD.

True. "Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel" (Joshua 24:31). The promise made at Shechem held through Joshua's days and the elders' days. That beats my track record with New Year's resolutions, friend.

The text says it did hold. "Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel" (Joshua 24:31). So the people kept serving through Joshua's days and the elders' days. Keeping a promise for that long is no small thing, baker.
